extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, writers, and creators interested in Substack and online newsletter platforms
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia company article summarizing Substack's history, features, business model, content policies, programs, and notable criticism — useful for creators, journalists, and researchers evaluating the platform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content moderation policy — prohibited content
rubrics_metrics.description: Substack's content moderation policy includes rules against 'harassment, threats, spam, pornography, and calls for violence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy is described as 'lightweight'; moderation decisions are made by the founders. The company has been criticized for allowing extremist content and for taking a minimal-censorship approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content moderation stance — minimal censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Founders affirmed a commitment to minimal censorship, arguing 'Society has a trust problem. More censorship will only make it worse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stance has led to controversy and criticism (e.g., permitting authors accused of misinformation or extremist views), creators leaving the platform, and public debates about the platform's responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creator ownership and revenue share
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers own their newsletters; Substack usually takes a 10% cut from subscription payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can choose free or paid subscriptions and control which posts are publicly available to non-subscribers. For some deals (e.g., comics signings) Substack takes 10% after the creator's first year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription pricing policy (historical minimum)
rubrics_metrics.description: As of 2020, the minimum subscription fee was $5/month or $30/year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators decide pricing for their newsletters; the platform's stated minimum and percentage cut affect creator revenue and business decisions. (The page cites this as the minimum 'as of 2020'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization features and supported content types
rubrics_metrics.description: Substack provides infrastructure for subscription-based content including newsletters, podcasts, video, livestreams, Notes (short-form posts), group chats, and a TV app.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeline/examples: podcast support added in 2019; Notes introduced in 2023; Substack Reader apps for iOS/Android; video, livestreaming, and Substack TV introduced by 2026; Spotify distribution partnership and tools for podcasters; creators may monetize these formats subject to platform terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creator programs and financial support (Substack Pro, fellowships, grants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substack experimented with Substack Pro, a revenue-sharing program that paid advances to writers; the program was criticized for lack of disclosure and ended in 2022. Substack also ran fellowships/grants and provided advances to some creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs included $3,000 stipends and workshops (fellowship), $1,000–$3,000 grants after the pandemic, and advances to attract creators. These programs have been sources of both recruitment and controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal support program (Substack Defender)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substack provides legal advice to its writers through Substack Defender: lawyers review stories before publication and advise on cease-and-desist letters; Substack committed to covering up to $1 million in fees for cases accepted by Defender lawyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The program was expanded in 2025 to include a partnership with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE). This is a creator-facing safety/defense benefit with eligibility/process implied by 'cases accepted by Defender lawyers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical content mix on the platform
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Substack newsletters offer personal writing, opinion pieces, research, and analysis; 'few of its newsletters publish original reporting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers (e.g., The New Yorker) noted this content profile as characteristic of the platform, which may inform expectations for creators or readers seeking investigative reporting versus opinion/personal work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and privacy handling (incidents and response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substack has experienced privacy/security incidents (e.g., exposing email addresses in a 2020 email, disclosed 2025 security breach affecting emails, phone numbers, and metadata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The company acknowledged mistakes, fixed issues, and announced investigations to prevent recurrence. Security history is a consideration for creators deciding where to host subscriber data.
